utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we begin today, the Chamber will issue two oral rulings. The Chamber will first issue an oral decision on the Prosecution request in relation to the status of Exhibit P71 filed on the 16th of October, 2012. In the request, the Prosecution notes that Exhibit P71 is identified on the Registry's exhibit list as confidential and asks that Exhibit P71 remain under seal and that a public redacted version of P71 uploaded to e-court under Rule 65 ter number 90047A be admitted into evidence. On the 17th of October, 2012, the accused's legal adviser informed the Chamber by e-mail that the accused does not oppose the Prosecution's request in the motion. The Chamber notes that P71, a witness statement for Safeta Hamzic, was provisionally admitted into evidence on 10th of November, 2009, pursuant to Rule 92 bis subject to the Prosecution complying with the formal requirements of Rule 92 bis (B). On the 19th of November, 2010, the Prosecution informed the Chamber that the attestation procedure for the witness statement of Safeta Hamzic had been completed. On the 10th of December, 2010, the Chamber admitted P71 into evidence as a public exhibit. The Chamber recalls its decisions of 10th of November, 2009, and 10th of December, 2010, whereby it admitted P71 publicly and notes that the Registry's exhibit list is incorrect in that respect. The Chamber therefore understands the request to be a motion for reconsideration of the public status of P71. Given the Prosecution's submissions in the request and in accordance with the practice in this case, the Chamber is not satisfied that it is necessary to reconsider the public status of P71 to prevent injustice. The Chamber, therefore, denies the Prosecution's request to place Exhibit P71 under seal and to admit a public redacted version and requests the Registry to mark P71 as public in e-court. Next could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we bring in the next witness. I take it the next witness is Mr. Veljovic?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, a small correction to the transcript from yesterday. Page number 29179, line 8, currently the exhibit number listed there is Exhibit D2334. Instead it should read Exhibit D2344. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, have you read the printed version of your statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read a short summary of Mr. Veljovic's statement in English. [In English] Stevan Veljovic was an operative officer in the 1st Romanija Brigade during the war. Long before the outbreak of the conflict, he had learnt about the formation of paramilitary Muslim units and their secret arming, while in late 1990 and during 1991 this was no secret anymore. At this time they began forming the main bodies of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. By 1991, inter-ethnic division was pervasive. In early 1992 Muslims who were in the Patriotic League started openly controlling roads in the municipality. They would stop vehicles and search them as well as the passengers for weapons. Stevan Veljovic was mobilised to the 216th Mountain Brigade on 30th of June, 1991, and was the assistant commander for operations and training. This mobilisation was boycotted by most of the Muslims. By 18th [sic] of May 1992 an agreement had been reached about the pullout of JNA units from BH. He was tasked to move the unit to the Lukavica barracks. Before the unit's departure to this location, Muslim and Croatian officers and soldiers left the unit. As of September 1992, local battalions whose function was to protect the Serbian villages around Sarajevo and which were manned exclusively by local inhabitants were included in the composition of the brigade. The brigade was armed with establishment infantry weapons. The unit had snipers, but they were insufficiently trained reservists, so they used sniper rifles like standard weapons rather than sniper rifles. Training of sniper instructors was organised as late as 1995 on the order of the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. His unit had numerous problems with the logistics support. Supply routes were frequently controlled and covered by enemy fire. They were constantly short of shells for the support equipment. The combat lines of the 1st Corps of BH army were very close to his unit's defence positions and were often separated by one street. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and its soldiers shared the same strategy: To guard and protect Serbian settlements, their families and property in the zone of defence of the brigade. This is why offensive operations were never carried out, but merely defensive ones. They were aware that if the forces of the 1st Corps of BH army broke through any segment of their line of the defence, it would have freed up numerous and serious [sic] enemy forces. Muslim forces were positioned in various features that were dominant in relation to his unit's line of defence and from which they constantly shelled and inflicted casualties, especially in Grbavica and Nedzarici. Neither the brigade nor any of its organs ordered shelling of civilians or civilian buildings, only military targets and only when under artillery and infantry fire from the Muslim side. Even though they knew that Muslim units and equipment often used civilian buildings as shelter. Muslim forces used important cultural, social, historical, health, commercial, and civilian facilities or were positioned near UN monitoring forces, with the strategy of Chetniks being immediately accused of deliberately destroying those buildings when they did return fire at such targets. There had been several orders from the -- all Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command levels that fire was to be opened only if lives were directly threatened, and only at targets endangering the security of the unit. Neither he nor his unit ever had the intention during combat to cause civilian casualties or to terrorise civilians. It was prohibited to fire at civilians, civilian facilities, and means of public transport. He never issued orders in that sense nor did his unit receive such orders. Stevan Veljovic stated that his brigade constantly respected all truces, unlike the Muslim forces, which persistently violated them. UN observers were alongside them at all times and they could see this for themselves. He drafted numerous regular and interim combat reports for the brigade -- for his brigade that clearly shows that they were constantly attacked and shelled and thus forced to return fire. Regarding humanitarian aid, convoys frequently passed through his unit's zone of responsibility and were never obstructed in any way, unless they were transporting at the same time items intended for military use. In early August 1995, Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was recognised -- reorganised and he was appointed commander of the 4th Sarajevo Brigade. He then detached and intervention platoon and the entire 220- [sic] and 80-millimetre mortar battery was sent to Trebinje front to assist in the defence of the Herzegovina Corps of the VRS against forces of Republic of Croatia. After that, there was no support equipment left in his brigade. Therefore, in this connection to the Markale II incident, he maintains that at that time there was not a single 120-millimetre mortar on that direction. Thank you. [Interpretation] At this stage I have no questions for Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You've testified previously at this Tribunal, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the month of May in 1997 in the General Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In fact, it wasn't actually 1997, it was 2007, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In 2007, yes, I testified in the Milosevic case. It started in the month of May. I was here from the 22nd of May to the 1st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you say "the Milosevic case," you refer to General Dragomir Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: General Dragomir Milosevic. I was an operative in the corps from 1994, from the month of December, up to August 1995. That's why I testified in his case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So can you confirm then something that wasn't mentioned in your statement related to this. General Milosevic was also your commander in the 216th Mountain Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it was under his command that you and other soldiers in the 216th Brigade moved to Sarajevo in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Correct. We moved to Sarajevo in 1992 from the Drina river sector. We were a unit of the JNA and we had to obey orders issued by the JNA. We were moved to Sarajevo because we had manpower and assets which could help people move from the barracks in Sarajevo. We could also provide them with fuel. We arrived in Sarajevo on the 3rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who was your operations commander in the 216th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That was me at the beginning of the war and before the war it was a Muslim, Nehru Ganic, and then he defected and joined the BiH army and now he is a BiH general.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the 1st Romanija Brigade you continued to serve under Dragomir Milosevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. General Milosevic was appointed by the government, i.e., by the ministry of Republika Srpska as the commander of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. And then he selected officers who would compose his brigade. Many had by then left for Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Milosevic moved in February 1993 to serve with the Drina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he went to the Drina Corps for chief of the operations sector of the Drina Corps, and Colonel --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- came to replace him as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It was actually Vlado Lizdek that came to replace him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in the 1st Romanija Brigade, who was your operations commander?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It was me right until 1994 when on the 19th of December, 1994, I came to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps as an operative officer because Commander Milosevic was already appointed and he called me to become the operations officer of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Milosevic called you to become operations officer. How -- was that a phone call? Was that an appointment? How did it happen?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: He issued an order that I should come for that duty, and so I reported pursuant to this order. Well, since he knew me from before, he provided me with this opportunity, or rather, this post because I knew how to do this job.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as operations officer within the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps you were part of the staff of the corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as part of the corps staff, and Colonel Cedomir Sladoje was my superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what was his position?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander and Chief of Staff at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe since you were in the corps staff I can read you some names and you could tell me whether the names I give you were also members of the staff. How about Marko Lugonja?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Marko Lugonja, he was the assistant commander for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And as assistant commander for intelligence and security, he reported, I suppose, directly to the corps commander; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct that he was his assistant but they had separate channels. The security organ was connected with the Main Staff because the operatives have special powers.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who in the Main Staff or what organ in the Main Staff was Lugonja then connected to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: With General Tolimir who was Mladic's assistant for intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So he reported in two lines: Directly to the corps commander, General Milosevic, and also to General Tolimir; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the intelligence staff have a separate thing that they do it like that. Even though he was Milosevic's assistant, he was tightly connected to Tolimir. That's how it was in the Serbian army because this is approximately how these rules were adhered to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was Luka Dragicevic also a member of the corps staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Luka Dragicevic was in the corps staff. He was the assistant commander for morale and legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did he also have a separate reporting channel to the VRS Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not. He was responsible to General Milosevic but he also had some links with the assistant. They would meet from time to time. Security is something separate, special, and morale and legal affairs is not. This is how the intelligence people do it in order to gather data.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: When you say he also had some links with the assistant and they would meet from time to time, I take it you're referring to General Gvero?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, General Gvero. He was the assistant for morale at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Aleksa Krsmanovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Aleksa Krsmanovic was the assistant commander for logistics, for logistical units for provisions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This is supposed to be answer, not question, on line 13, 14.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Tadija Manojlovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Tadija Manojlovic was the chief of artillery at the corps staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was he linked with in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Of course he was linked with the chief of the artillery at the Main Staff. There are close links there. That is how the relations of subordination are in the army, from top towards the bottom and from the bottom up, in terms of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was the artillery chief in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Milan Ugresic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Milan Ugresic was the chief of anti-aircraft defence, the PVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Milja [phoen] Vlahovic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: He was the chief of engineering.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Dusan Josipovic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Dusan Josipovic was the chief of communications.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And Milivoj Solar, who was he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Milivoj Solar was a Croat. He was in our corps. He was the chief of the technical service which was attached to the logistics sector, so Aleksa Krsmanovic was his boss.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What are the technical services?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Logistics comprises the technical service, the medical corps, and the quartermasters sections. That is -- those comprise the logistics section.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, we'll come back to that, your time in the corps staff. But I want to go and look a little bit at your job description, if I can call it that, back down in the brigade level. And tell me if I'm correct. Part of your job as operations officer within the brigade was to receive and collate reports from the battalions and their subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: An operations officer in the brigade or in the corps is someone who deals with combat issues, works on the war and military skills, makes and sends reports to the commander, and they can also receive command assignment. He can be given two battalions and command them. They also draft TKT documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your job with the Romanija Brigade, did you receive reports from the battalions and their subordinate units, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if you weren't there for one reason or another, did you have a duty officer who collected information on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We had duty officers, but the operations officer was always informed about it and the Chief of Staff. I'm talking about the battalion reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the reports that you'd receive at brigade level would come in from all the units - am I right? - the companies, the battalions, the platoons, and the squads?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, they would only come from the battalions and the artillery division and the staff units, such as the smaller units, engineers, communications, the staff units --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can you just repeat your last sentence, please, after "staff units."

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The companies would send reports to battalion commanders or to the batteries, then to the division commander, and then the komandirs of the platoons and the companies, signals, and so on, and then the communications company commander, which was a staff unit, would send his reports to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do not overlap while the interpreters are interpreting. Yes, we couldn't hear your words, Mr. Karadzic. What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mike.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the answer in line 23 something has been mixed up. The witness said that the companies and the batteries in the artillery would send reports to their first superiors, and here it seems as if they were sending it to the battalion commanders or to the batteries. Perhaps we could ask the witness to speak slowly because he said company or a battery at the same level and then above that it was their superiors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The brigade command would receive reports from battalion commanders and commanders of batteries and independent staff units, while battalions comprised companies and divisions comprised batteries, and they and the companies are receiving to the division and the companies are receiving to the battalions and the battalion comprises all of that and sends it to the brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the reports that the brigades received, did they come orally or in writing or both?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It would receive oral reports, but there had to be a written report in the evening which would be sent to the brigade; and then the brigade would send it to the corps and this would be an encrypted report. The corps would send it to the Main Staff and the Main Staff would send it to the Supreme Command, and that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: To do this job the brigade, I take it, had communications with the operations officers and centres at the subordinate level; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The brigade had a system of communications and it had links with the battalions, and then in turn the battalions had links with the companies, and the brigade had links with the corps, the corps had links with the Main Staff, and the Main Staff with the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, these reports that went from the brigade level up to the corps command, who approved them before they were sent?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Every report would be signed by the corps commander or by somebody standing in for him on that day if the commander -- if the corps commander was absent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I asked you about the brigade level command -- the brigade level reports that went up to the corps command and your answer talked about reports that went from the corps command further up to the Main Staff. But just to fill this in, who at the brigade level approved the reports before they went to the corps command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: 90 per cent or 100 per cent the brigade commander; if the brigade commander was not there, the Chief of Staff; if the Chief of Staff was not there, then the operations officer would sign it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You said that these reports would have to go in written form to the corps command in the evening. What was the dead-line for sending that -- those reports in?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: By 8.00 in the evening they would be sent, by 2000 hours at the latest they would be sent. There were also extraordinary reports if something happened unforeseen, then the extraordinary report would also be sent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And would you do an updated report in the morning?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, not in the morning. Only in the evening when the operations officer would write the report, then the commander would update it. If he didn't like something, if something was not done properly, then he would ask to have that corrected. It would be corrected and then he would approve it, send it and -- sign it and send it to the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. So you've already given evidence just a few minutes ago that once these reports arrived in the corps operations section, they'd be sent further on to the Main Staff. What was the dead-line, the daily dead-line, for doing that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The daily dead-line was in the evening, by 9.00 p.m., that's the time by which the Main Staff had to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And what about the other -- when we're talking about reports sent to the Main Staff, what about the other sections? Did those daily operations reports contain reports from the other sectors we've just talked about, artillery, security, morale, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It all had to be there, artillery, firing, enemy fire, our fire, everything that was done that day had to be put in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And there was a -- you've alluded to a link between some of the other sectors and the Main Staff. Did they also -- did those sectors, security, for example, also generate separate reports for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I never did any intelligence work but I was involved in operations and command, I did not really have much to do with the intelligence tasks. I wasn't permitted to do that and I wasn't able to do that, and that wasn't part of my duties either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I just asked you about reporting. Did the other sectors also generate separate reports for the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, just one report would be drafted, but the intelligence section had a separate channel. They would compile data regarding the units. They did the security and intelligence for the units and that is why they were treated as a special service, intelligence and security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to another area just to clarify some things from your statement. I just want to talk about the Romanija Brigade's command. You said in your statement that it was located in three places, Tilava, the Bob facility --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: 1st Romanija.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Bob facility and Miljevici. So until when were you at Miljevici?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Every brigade command has its command post and it also has a forward command post. Miljevici and Bog were a forward command post where you would have an operations officer or some other duty officers, and then the main command post would be located in the rear. There could also be a number of forward command posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Tilava was your main command post; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the beginning, but this actually changed several times.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where were you in 1993 -- where was the brigade's command post in 1993?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In 1993 the brigade command post was in Ljubogosta in autumn in a restaurant or cafe. This was in the municipality of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in 1994 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In 1995 the 1st Brigade command was at the Nisicka Visoraban [phoen] elevation and there was a command post in Jahorina in 1993. The command post switched locations frequently because of security.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And depending on the operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll move on. So back to the corps again. As a member of the corps staff you became familiar with how the corps staff worked, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I took part in the planning of the work of the corps for certain periods of time and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And those -- that planning work was prepared according to directors' directives and orders from your superior command?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Exactly. Every army -- I mean, we're soldiers, we draft plans, we make certain predictions, estimates, we make plans, and it's quite another thing whether those plans will be implemented or not. What else could they do other than draft tactical moves or deal with tactics when we're talking about one army against another.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How often in a day did the commander, General Milosevic, meet with his corps staff?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: General Milosevic would have a briefing every morning. He would provide certain guide-lines regarding the line of defence of the brigade in order to have an overview of certain jobs in the field, the correction of certain tactical positions and so on. And then in the evening we would report back about what we did and what the staff officers did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you had these daily meetings, were the sector assistants also present?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were obliged to attend, the sector assistants, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If you needed to get information for these meetings from the subordinate units, how would you do that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The intelligence and security organ provided a lot of information about the enemy, and that was their assignment. The operations and training organ cannot work unless they have intelligence information from the intelligence and security organ. They had their scouts, observers, and they reported information so that we could set up the best possible defence in case something was being prepared. If some actions of theirs were being prepared, then we would be able to respond to that since the entire time we were in the defensive and not in the offensive.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was the Chief of Staff always present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. The Chief of Staff is the one who leads the staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm afraid you were speaking a little bit too quickly and softly and the interpreter didn't hear your answer after: "Of course. The Chief of Staff is the one who leads the staff." Could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The corps command has the corps commander and his assistants for security, for logistics, for morale, and the Chief of Staff is in charge of the services, the artillery, the engineers, the infantry communications, and so on, and so he is their head. I hope that's clear now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Cedo Sladoje was always present at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Cedo Sladoje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if for some reason General Milosevic wasn't present, who led the meetings, Cedo Sladoje?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was also his deputy at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So would it be true then that the commander and the Chief of Staff would co-ordinate their actions?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. They would meet very often, eyeball to eyeball, and they would discuss certain things in order to make the staff briefings as efficient as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if for some reason both the commander, General Milosevic and Cedo Sladoje, weren't available, who then led the meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: One of the assistants, the assistant -- assistant's corps commander or in some cases the operative because the operative was also the deputy Chief of Staff. The chief operative was also the deputy Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So decisions were made at these meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And orders were issued at these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. And that's true for all the armies of this world; right?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And notes or minutes were kept of these meetings, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Minutes were kept at each meeting. Tasks were issued, those were recorded by one of the officers who was in charge of keeping the minutes. It would usually be the chief for morale. And also it was recorded what was implemented and what was not. That's why every word was recorded and this helped when it came to monitoring what was achieved and what was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Luka Dragicevic was the one who kept the minutes and notes of these meetings?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Luka Dragicevic as well as Milan Ugresic because he kept very good minutes. But the commander would appoint the person. If somebody had a bad handwriting, they would obviously not be in charge of keeping the minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the operations section, your section, sometimes took minutes -- the minutes of those meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. He recorded everything that the commander said in order to undertake operative and defensive measures in the unit. If some other more common things were discussed, such as supplies or assignments, then he would not record that -- those.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. So how often -- or maybe you can confirm this: The corps commander would also meet his brigade commanders as a group, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very often the corps commander had briefings with the brigade commanders, but that was not that often. It was once a week or once in a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: As a brigade operations officers and as corps operations officer, you would have attended those briefings on both ends, wouldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I attended and I also kept minutes. I recorded what the brigade commander said, what tasks they were given. I kept those minutes and I also monitored the implementation of those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you would have done that at both the brigade and corps level, wouldn't you have?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Those meetings would also have included the regiment commanders; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, independent regiments. There was a mixed artillery regiment, there was a mixed anti-tank regiment, the PVO regiment, the commander of the military police, the staff units at the corps, the chief of engineers, the engineering battalion, they were at the level of the brigade commanders. Those were the so-called independent units that belonged to the corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What about these brigades that you've referred to in your statement, the Trebevic Battalion, the Jahorina Battalion, Podgrab Battalion, those were also independent -- so-called independent units that belonged to the corps, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, they belonged to the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade and later, after the reorganisation, they were given to the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. That's who they were assigned to. They were never independent. They were always elements of a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now talking about the brigades, I saw that you mentioned in your statement that the zone of responsibility of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade was Zlatiste on the right and Djukica Potok on the left, and as far back as Tilava, and Tvrdemici, but this Chamber has already heard evidence that Zlatiste, for example, was in the area of responsibility of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. Did they assume responsibility for that area after it was held by your brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They took the responsibility over from us. At first it was our zone, Zlatiste on the right, Djukica Potok on the left, and Tilava in-depth. But a zone of responsibility is in-depth and in width. And then when we were joined by the three battalions, namely, Paljevine [phoen], Jahorina, Podgrab, and Kresani. Then we -- i.e., General Lizdek assigned two battalions from Grbavica to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, and then our zone of responsibility was from Trebinac to -- or Bistica [phoen] brook Vidikovac and to Radovan. In-depth, the villages of Rakulic [phoen] and Mokra and Romanija. The zone changed depending on the composition of the brigade. Sometimes things overlapped and that's why you are puzzled about the fact that at one point our zone of responsibility belonged to the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. It did happen over time. The composition of the brigade would change and the zone would change slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Who commanded the Novo Sarajevo Brigade of the Territorial Defence that you referred to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The Novo Sarajevo brigade was under the command of a person who is no longer amongst the living. His name was Obradovic. He was killed during the war. Pod [phoen] Obradovic was his name. That was the Territorial Defence of the Serbian army, i.e., the Serbian guards. When the Republika Srpska army arrived, it was ordered that those brigades should join our brigade as battalions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And who was Radomir Kojic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Radomir Kojic was a policeman at the beginning of the war. And then on the 31st of October or thereabouts in 1992 when commander -- the commander of the Trebevic Battalion Milorad Lolovic was killed, he was appointed as the commander of the Trebevic Battalion which was an element of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did it remain in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It remained in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade up to the 7th August 1995. And for only two months they belonged to the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. And then the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade was set up, and then that changed because the 1st Romanija Brigade went to Nisici and there was a sort of an interregnum before the new 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade was set up. In any military there are very frequently changes, very frequent manoeuvres, hence all the subsequent changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So -- maybe so we can get this straight in my mind I can have you look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter number 09390G, please. Can we blow that up a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, I wonder if -- because I'd like to see this in -- more visually laid out, I wonder if you can mark on this map the area of responsibility of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade after it absorbed these independent units, and I accept that we might have lost a bit of territory on the east side of Sarajevo. Can you mark that? Can you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry that we're in the courtroom and we're discussing military issues without the original maps of the 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. A map is one of the most important elements of the military because the map reflects everything that we did. You would see the deployment of both forces. When the Milosevic trial was on we saw the map of the 1st Corps map by General Karavelic, we also saw our map, and we could not lie about any of the zones of responsibility. We knew exactly where the units were and this is a very small scale and I cannot observe, I cannot notice everything. It's not visible to -- the red line here, usually it is done on a map who -- which -- with a scale of 1:50.000. I can't see Grbavica here at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Can we make it a little bit smaller for Mr. Veljovic. And you had previously magnified it one time which looked pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Does that help you, Mr. Veljovic, or would you like it one bigger?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I can't see anything in the south-east. You can't see anything from the Miljacka river. There are no lines there. I can see Trebevic. I understand the map because a map represents everything that is on the ground, forests, meadows. I am sorry that there's no expert in the courtroom who could correct me if I misspeak. When it comes to the 1st Romanija Brigade, this is Grbavica to Djukica Potok and across Trebevic and below the road that leads through the forested part of Trebevic all the way up to Mrkovici here. However, I cannot see Mrkovici here at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, would you like us to make it -- to magnify it once more for you? That's no problem. Because, Mr. Veljovic, you were there, so you would be in the ideal position to indicate your brigade's zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- but I can't see anything here on this map. This map is not the original map that was drafted by the corps. Throughout the other trial we had it in the courtroom -- during the Milosevic and Galic's trials you could see both sides, our side and the enemy's side. You could see the deployment of all the units at every observation point, the artillery positions, anti-aircraft positions. And when you can see that, you know that we cannot lie because that map contained everything. Because whatever the Muslims drew up on their side we copied on our side. I'm sorry that you can't show me that map -- those maps, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What's your concern with marking this map? You said just now that we cannot lie with a pre-marked map, referring to one you had seen in your previous trial. What's --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I can't see well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Magnify it, please, one more time and then we'll see what can happen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see the Zeljo pitch, Grbavica, the Jewish cemetery, I can't see all that on this map. I can't even see Trebevic. I don't know where Trebevic is.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One more time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The scale is too small. It's impossible for any operative to use a map of this kind, to work with a map of this kind. Now I might be able to draw something perhaps.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be provided with a pen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now this has to be moved, you have to move the map because -- move it to the left, to the left.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll have to have him --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: We'll have to have you initial and date this, please, Mr. Veljovic, before we move it to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll ask him to draw again. We move the map --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the zone of responsibility, not all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Move to the left, move the map to the left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will lose your marking already, but why don't we do that. We can lose this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can delete it. Whatever.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So at this magnification if we could just move the map to the left so the witness can see the east side of the city, and further east, please. Further east, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you wait until assisted by our usher, please. Is this map okay, Mr. Veljovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] More to the left. More to the left. More to the left. More to the left. More and more to the left. There you go. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If he can be helped with his pen now. I think Mr. Veljovic can sketch out the area of responsibility of the 1st Romanija Brigade after they had absorbed these battalions he referred to in his statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the previous line has been erased so I don't know. Again you have to move the map so that I can find Radava which is at the top part of the map. Move the map closer to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, this clearly doesn't suit the witness and I think we'll move on and perhaps over the break we can get him a hard copy so he can have a look at this. I don't want to spend any more time in court on this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's the way to go. Give me a copy on paper and I will draw anything you want me to draw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. But I was wondering whether we could not use the map prepared by the SRK, which we saw earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the way, the -- yes, that's the map. That's the map I need and want. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll look into it and let Your Honours know after the next break if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How much longer would you need to conclude your cross-examination, Ms. Edgerton, after the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The next session after that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, since we do have another witness here today and we're not scheduled to be in session again until next Tuesday, could the Chamber look into potentially extending the sitting for today's session so that we could complete that witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe shorter [In English] Or not to start. A little longer so to release the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just speaking for myself, I wondered why you would need all that hours to examine such a thing with this witness, but how much would you expect for the next witness, Mr. Tieger? Is it you that would cross-examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's also me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I actually think we would be able to be done with both of them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I mean -- I'm speaking somewhat optimistically, but I would make all efforts to be done with both of them today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So there's one matter I would like to deal with in private session in the absence of the witness. So, Mr. Veljovic, we'll take a break for half an hour, so you may be excused now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will take a break for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, just one question on the subject of reports that I actually omitted to sort of finish off with. These reports that you said at the corps were prepared to go to the Main Staff, who drafted those? Was it the operations section?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was the operations section that on the whole drafted those reports in 99 per cent of the cases. The corps commander would then send them, having read it, and then they would be sent to the superior command for encoding.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now to go on to another subject that you added to your statement and you -- in the version that you signed, you added a paragraph about Faletici saying that in April 1992 members of the Patriotic League and Green Berets started driving weapons from Faletici away. Where did you get that information?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's because the 216th Brigade was part of the JNA at the time. We received an order to protect that warehouse so that it didn't fall into the hands of the Green Berets; in other words, to prevent them from seizing the weapons. The 216th Brigade was part of the JNA at the time and we received the -- an order to protect the warehouse, to ensure that weapons of the Territorial Defence for the town of Sarajevo were not seized because there were a lot of rifles and other materiel and technical and military equipment in that warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you were there; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 216th Brigade was at the site, and on that occasion we clashed with the Patriotic League and the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you know who Milovan Bjelica is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I know who Milovan Bjelica is. He's from Sokolac. He's also a relative of mine because his father and my mother -- brother and sister.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you know who Jovan Bartula is?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Jovan Bartula, at the beginning of the war he was in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps where he had the duty of a commander of a mixed anti-armoured regiment.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I'd like to go to 65 ter number 12028. It's a copy of an interview that Milovan Bjelica gave to Srpsko Oslobodjenje on 27 December 1994. And I think that the far right-hand column on this first page is -- I'll just -- your indulgence for a moment. The far right-hand column towards the bottom is the one that should be enlarged for Mr. Veljovic. Mr. Veljovic, Milovan Bjelica in this interview says that he was also there and said that in answer to the question: "How did you arm the people?" Milovan Bjelica said: "And our greatest success was taking the weapons -- the equipment and weapons from Faletici" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: English page.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honours. English page 3. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He's then asked the question: "You did it right in front of the enemy, under sniper rifle?" And he answers: "We stole it from their hands. We agreed with the then-minister of defence and with a man from security of the then-Sarajevo Corps." It was: "Gagovic was there as well. We did it by night in April 1992. We entered with hundred trucks on the first night. There was a group of young men, activists of SDS which I was leading, and also a group from Pale from the party led by Radomir Kojic, then unit of current Colonel Jovan Bartula, then Ilija Maletic with his people from Stari Grad. This depot contained all weapons of the Territorial Defence of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. We raided in there the first night and as soon as we entered the depot, the Green Berets and special forces of Dragan Bikic started surrounding the barracks." And further he says: "We repelled the attack and started pulling out the weapons. The first night, we took whole artillery and weapons. There was about 300 artillery tubes from 35- to 50.000 rifles as well as other equipment." And further he says: "We were helped by the unit of Colonel Dragoljub Milosevic, i.e., the 1st Romanija Brigade ... and we brought all weapons and equipment to the territory of Romanija in three days." So, Mr. Veljovic, it seems that Mr. Bjelica your relative was also there and contradicts your assertion about events in Faletici.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see Mr. Bjelica. He was there daily or a day later. When the 216th Brigade arrived there, I did not see Milovan Bjelica or Radomir Kojic on that day. We had between 600 and 700 soldiers. We helped to protect the warehouse. We got some of the weapons out and placed them in Mokro, in the barracks. And I don't know where some of the other weapons went towards Sokolac I think. These were the weapons of the Territorial Defence staff, not of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but of the town of Sarajevo. As for this report, or rather, article, it's the first time I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I take it from your answer you don't dispute what Mr. Bjelica says happened?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Not a hundred per cent. But it's true that we got a lot of the weapons out of the Faletici warehouse and, as I said, we placed them in the barracks in Mokro in some warehouses in Sokolac because they attacked the warehouse first and then we protected it. The Green Berets and the Patriotic League also took quite a few weapons from the warehouse in Faletici. Everyone was trying to grab these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. This is the statement of a third party and she'll have another opportunity to tender this during later Defence witnesses, particularly KW-38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness confirmed to a certain extent that they took a lot of the weapons out of that Faletici warehouse. Do we need to admit it separately, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just a couple of questions about Dragomir Milosevic. You've said that you knew him quite well, and in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony you said you toured the combat lines with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I visited the lines with him. I was an operations training officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, he was regularly on the front lines. You told the Chambers in the Dragomir Milosevic case that he went to every trench along the front line, not once but several times.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: He was a field man and he was continually paying visits to the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you came here to testify in his defence, you knew what he was charged with at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew what he had been charged with.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you knew that just like Dr. Karadzic he was charged with a 120-millimetre mortar shelling in Sarajevo on 28 August 1995 that killed 43 and injured 75; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of August, 1995, Milosevic wasn't in command of the corps. He had been wounded and he was at the military medical academy. And Cedo Sladomir [as interpreted], Colonel Cedo Sladomir [as interpreted] was replacing him, so Milosevic wasn't present when Markale was shelled. In the judgement you can see that he was liberated. Karavelic, the commander of the 1st Corps, also confirmed this in his order of the 26th. He confirmed that the citizens and troops should be protected because Cedo Sladoje would be shelling the town of Sarajevo. But they allowed for the market, but I don't think that a shell can fall on Markale because 120- and 82-millimetre mortar, well, these are weapons that I know very well. And in order to hit such a location -- well that is simply impossible. I'd stake my life on that and I would go as far as standing at that site and being shelled there. We didn't have any mortars on Trebevic in 1995 because it's covered by forest. There aren't very suitable positions for firing positions. All the mortars were withdrawn because there was an order from Cedo Sladoje, according to which some of the SRK forces should be sent to Trebinje. And my unit in the event of an attack would be supported by --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- a corps -- by the corps artillery --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, Mr. Veljovic, I asked you a simple question. You knew that Dragomir Milosevic was charged with exactly the same incident that Dr. Karadzic is here today; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And when you came to testify in General Milosevic's Defence, your testimony was specifically related to that incident; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You offered up an alibi for him?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And in fact in your testimony at those previous -- that previous trial, you actually never denied that the shell had fallen on the market-place on 28 August 1992 [sic], but you're doing it today?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I heard about that, since it was conveyed through the media. We asked for expert reports and we wanted to visit the site because at the time the army wasn't active. Only one shell was fired then. It seems it hit Markale, the market, and caused a massacre. And I said --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: -- said that General Milovanovic --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, when you testified before the Trial Chamber in the Dragomir Milosevic case, you didn't deny that the incident had happened, but today you are. Which testimony are we supposed to rely on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Ms. Edgerton, could you clarify your statement that he didn't deny that the incident had happened. Do you mean that he admitted that it was fired by the Serb Sarajevo-Romanija Corps members?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, his testimony was specifically focused on General Dragomir Milosevic's absence from the theatre at that time, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether by saying that he didn't deny the incident, that he -- did he admit that it was done by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: He made no specific admission one way or another, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So could then -- could you reformulate your question. Yes, Mr. Robinson, before I ask -- I give the floor back to Ms. Edgerton, did you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I did, but you took the words out of my mouth so it's not necessary for me to say anything anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes -- pardon me. Your indulgence for just a second, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In your testimony here at this Tribunal in the Dragomir Milosevic case, you didn't mention the evidence you've now offered in your signed statement to the effect that you had 120-millimetre mortar battery on your command operating on the slopes of Trebevic and it was sent by you to Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we sent the battery to Trebinje before the 28th, around the 23rd, and they returned sometime in mid-September. We believed in our opinion we hadn't fired that shell. It had been planted and activated by a remote control. That was our opinion. Our opinion was that the Muslim forces had done this for propaganda purposes in order to ensure that we were bombed. In the Milosevic case I did not say anything about Markale as far as I know, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, you're clearly familiar with the incident. It's one of the --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'm familiar with it but I wasn't questioned about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: In the Milosevic case, when I testified in that case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Because I wasn't in the corps then. I was in the 4th Brigade and I wasn't asked about Markale.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your testimony -- let me try again. This incident is one of the single-most controversial events in the history of the conflict around Sarajevo, and in the Dragomir Milosevic case you were testifying at what might have been the last opportunity to provide that evidence. And you're saying now it didn't even occur to you to bring it up?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I object to -- excuse me, Mr. Veljovic. Hold on one second, please. One second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, that's a question to which the answer would have absolutely no probative value. He's not in control of what he can give -- what is the subjects of his testimony. And if the lawyers for General Milosevic or the Prosecutor chose not to ask him about that, there's nothing that reflects on his credibility from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the witness said, Ms. Edgerton, that he was not asked about that. Could you start from the actual transcript or reformulate your question, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In the transcript in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony you talked specifically about your command of the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade. You said it was established on the 7th of August. You explained how you incorporated the Trebevic Battalion and other brigades. You said I didn't have enough support artillery and I had to rely on the corps artillery. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we be provided with a reference?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do remember that. Since the 4th Brigade was established late there were only firing groups and we didn't have the possibility of forming a brigade artillery group. And therefore, I had to rely on the corps artillery group that was to the east, on the opposite side from Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, please wait when interpreters are continuing to interpret. Do not overlap, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought they had finished because the transcript had come to an end. Line 17, the witness said that there were only battalion firing groups in existence, and "battalion" is missing. It hasn't been entered in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your indulgence for a moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I asked for a reference for the Milosevic testimony that Ms. Edgerton was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Transcript page 5834, 5835.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: You had the opportunity in these proceedings to talk about that mortar battery, and you -- are you asserting now the only reason why you chose not to raise it is because you weren't asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, Mr. President, that's an unfair question to the witness. He doesn't have the opportunity to raise issues. He can only answer what he's asked. That's -- really, she's making a point that this is omitted from the Milosevic testimony and that's as far as she can go with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is. And perhaps we could have, in light of everything, 65 ter number 23851 shown to the witness. It's a report on the availability of ammunition and fuel for combat vehicles, and it's dated 31 August 1992. And -- pardon me, 1995. And if you go over to the second page of the document you see that it's signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Veljovic, this document lists a number of weapons and vehicles available to your unit, a T-55 tank, some self-propelled guns, and a number of mortars, including 120-millimetre mortars. It seems that this document dated 31 August 1995 puts in doubt your assertion that your brigade's mortar battery was out of the Sarajevo theatre.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you go back to the first page so that he could see the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's nothing surprising about this. I signed this. This is what I brigade had at its disposal at the time, although they were in Trebinje battle-field I counted them as our men [as interpreted]. That's why I made a list of the equipment that we had in order to be able to issue that equipment to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the note at item number 11 that you had 13, 120-millimetre mortar --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I had the Jahorina Battalion, the Podgrab Battalion, but I listed all this -- I listed all this here, all the equipment that belonged to a number of battalions was listed here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I comment on the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the 4th Sarajevo Light Brigade, all their weapons: The Trebevici Battalion is one segment, the Podgrabski Battalion is another segment, the Jahorina Battalion is another segment, then you have the units attached to HQ. That's why I made a list of all the materiel and equipment in order to be sure that I knew what we had. From the 31st of August I started making a list and on the 7th it was necessary for the brigade to be ready for combat, 31st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on to another topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 8 it says "as our men" [In English] "As our own." [Interpretation] I signed, or rather, I made a list of these weapons which were ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see that. Let's continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Another area that you spoke about in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony but also haven't mentioned here was related to the subject of modified air bombs. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So maybe I could put some propositions to you about modified air bombs. From your Dragomir Milosevic testimony you were quite familiar with them; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And is it true with respect to modified air bombs that you often heard the commander saying they shouldn't be used because of your safety and because they weren't technically perfected?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The air bombs with launchers were devised by craftsmen. They were not approved, they were not precise, and the elevation was determined based on the equipment on the lorry and the fuel that fuelled the air bombs. And that's -- they could be off target by as much as 2 kilometres. That's why we were not supposed to use them in urban areas. We were allowed to use them only in wider areas where the two armies were in contact but there were no civilians, not in urban areas because there was a risk that we might actually hit our own men or civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's true, isn't it, that air bombs are actually highly destructive?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from 250 to 500 kilogrammes or even up to 1.000 kilogrammes intending to be launched from aircraft; however, that civil war forced people to devise those launchers. But we were supposed to use those air bombs only in wilderness where there were no human settlements, where there was no habitation, and all they created was panic among the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's because, as you described them, they were completely inaccurate; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Completely inaccurate. They were not tested. Even some crews were killed and the commanders were taken to court because it did happen that those bombs actually exploded there and then when they were activated. Only some of the brigades had them, not all of them. Only a few brigades on the strength of the corps had those air bombs, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Where were the commanders taken to court?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I know that something happened in Vogosca and some squad commanders whose crews were killed were handed over to courts. I don't know what happened next. I don't know how many were found guilty. I haven't a clue. But I know that some crews were killed because of those air bombs that were activated on the spot because those air bombs were not technically perfected.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's true that their deployment and use was directed by the corps commander; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It would be either the corps commander or brigade commanders, but all that excluded urban settlements. They could be used only in wilderness, as it were, where there were no urban settlements.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The corps commander or the brigade commander would decide on these air bombs with the approval of the Main Staff; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know whether it would be on the approval of the Main Staff but that should have been the case because the Main Staff signed the order for them to be removed from Vogosca and they were responsible for air bombs because some sort of a protection was added onto them after they were delivered from the factory or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, in fact, there was a group within the corps staff who was specifically responsible for monitoring the use and information -- pardon me, implementation of the air bombs; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, most probably those were chiefs of artillery, but I am not aware of the existence of such a group.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've said that you didn't use these bombs on urban areas, but I want you to have a look at P1297. It's a document you actually saw during your previous testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case. Pardon me, I misspoke, P1782. It's a report from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command to the VRS Main Staff dated 7 April 1995. And on page 2 in both versions under the heading "Our Forces" you see the notation that: "In Ilidza one 120-millimetre mine was fired and one 250 kilogramme air bomb was launched in the centre of Hrasnica." This document appears to -- this document suggests that something else happened other than what you've said, Mr. Veljovic.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It is correct that I testified in the Milosevic case and that this order was shown to me. However, imagine an aerial bomb weighing 250 kilos with such a destructive power. Its detonation can be heard 60 kilometres away. Hrasnica is close to the airport and UNPROFOR sources would have recorded an event like that and most probably would -- they would have informed the Main Staff in Zagreb. And since they did not register that -- I saw this order in the Milosevic case and I saw the records from one date to another date, and they never mentioned anything of that kind happening in the territory of the city of Sarajevo, UNPROFOR never did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Are you then saying that this didn't happen?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It didn't happen. I saw UNPROFOR reports which were shown to me at the Milosevic case. They sent a report for a certain date. They said everything was calm in Sarajevo. Hrasnica is 50 -- 500 metres away from the airport, and you have to know that the detonation of such a bomb could not have been not heard, and they would have heard it, they would have informed somebody about it. They never did. This never happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, I'd actually like to show you who did get informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter number 16453.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But in that sentence, Mr. Veljovic, it refers to a Luna rocket. Do you understand what it is about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is the Muslims who mentioned that. The Muslim forces mentioned that it was a Luna rocket which weighs 200 kilogrammes. Actually, it contains 200 kilogrammes of explosive, but we didn't have that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a rocket 6 metres long. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps did not have such rockets at their disposal. I remember everything that I testified to in that case and what I'm saying now is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please move on, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. If we could go back to that 65 ter number 16453.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I'd like to show you who did get informed about this. This is a report from the Main Staff of the VRS to the president dated 7 April 1994 [sic]. And if we could go over to paragraph 3(B) in both documents, please. I think you just need to go -- thank you. And in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did you say "1994"? It should be 1995, the same date.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It should be indeed. Thank you. My apologies. Over to page 5 in the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this document talks about the situation in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and it says under heading 3(B): "Situation in the Corps: "The enemy activity was adequately responded to whereby an air bomb (250 kg) was launched on the centre of Hrasnica." And then says: "The units have been engaged on additional engineering work on the positions, monitoring of activities being undertaken by the enemy, and prevention of surprises." So this document says not only that Dr. Karadzic was informed and contradicts your assertion that it didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the Main Staff told the Supreme Command. I didn't know anything about that and that's why referred to the UNPROFOR report covering the four-day period which was relevant and coincided with this event, and for that period they stated that the situation in Sarajevo was calm.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But you've given evidence in the Dragomir Milosevic case that as a brigade operations officer you were completely aware of what was happening in the area of your brigade and as a corps operations officer you knew almost everything going on in your brigade. You've also given evidence today that the operations sector was involved in drafting these reports that went up to the VRS Main Staff and to the president. So what should we rely on, Mr. Veljovic?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I did not draft this report. I didn't know anything about an aerial bomb being launched. Only UNPROFOR could know about that and they were close by. If they confirmed that that was the case, then that was the case. However, the UNPROFOR did not say anything, that's why I didn't suffer any consequences when I testified in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
