utterances.text: So in contrast to what you said in the Milosevic case and what you've said today, that this bomb wasn't launched, you're now saying you didn't know anything about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. That's why I'm saying I told you that a detonation would have been heard at a distance of 60 kilometres. The airport was closed. The UNPROFOR soldiers were there. They would have heard it; however, they didn't hear anything. They said everything was calm, hence my statement. And I believe that you will find it on the Internet what I testified to in the Milosevic case, and I'm telling you why I testified the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one more thing then before we leave that point. I'll just remind you, Mr. Veljovic, of what you said in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And the reference for the record is 5936.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: In answer to a question from Judge Mindua you specifically said: "This aerial bomb was not launched, that's for sure." You no longer stand by what you said in the Milosevic case, do you?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I still stand by that, because I relied on the UNPROFOR report. I didn't know about that and I thought that the UNPROFOR recorded everything. If the UNPROFOR had recorded that I would have agreed. Since the UNPROFOR never recorded such a launch, based on that I stated that the launch never took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, I find it very difficult to follow what you are saying. I don't think you drafted any of the UNPROFOR reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. We saw the documents from UNPROFOR because I didn't remember that. Maybe I wasn't there on that day. Maybe I was absent. I'm telling you that the explosion didn't happen. If it had had -- if it had happened then they would have sent a report to their own staff, and then I would know that it did occur. However, I couldn't confirm because I did not know about it, I did not hear it, I was not informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a separate thing to say that it -- the aerial bomb was not launched at all from saying that you don't know. But even after having looked at the Sarajevo Corps document as well as the Main Staff document, which are saying to the effect that aerial bomb was launched, you are still saying that that bomb was not launched, which means that these two reports are -- were lying at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether they're there or not, but maybe. That moment I was not there so I was in no position to know that that bomb was launched. That's why I referred to the UNPROFOR report because they were close, and if the UNPROFOR had confirmed the launch then yes, it happened. However, if they didn't confirm the launch, then it didn't happen. I don't know who signed this on behalf of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I don't know who signed it on behalf of the Main Staff and who then sent it to President Karadzic. I don't know who signed this on behalf of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So to be sure, it is your submission that if the UNPROFOR report does not confirm the content of this document, this is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because maybe that day I was in Rogatica and that's why I did not know about that bomb. Maybe I was at home on furlough, and that's why I wanted to see the UNPROFOR report. I relied on the UNPROFOR report. If the UNPROFOR report confirmed that there was a launch, then yes; but they said it was calm so there was no launch. I wanted to see the UNPROFOR report, it was shown to me on the screen, and it stated that Sarajevo and Zepa were calm during that particular period on those days, the document was shown to me on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, back to you, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript, please. Line 5 witness said "I asked to see" not "I wanted to see." I asked to see. [Interpretation] "I asked to see."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have that 65 ter number, I think it was 16453, tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Robinson, no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted as next Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5943, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And before it slips my mind completely, 65 ter number 23851, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P5944 , Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I think before we break one last area.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, you said in your statement that with respect to Bascarsija, paragraph I think it was 27, that you could have destroyed that part of the city with artillery but we never even tried to do that although we knew they were military targets and you received strict orders that that part of the city was never to be shelled under any circumstances. Now, that was in the context of a discussion or you dealt with this matter in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony as well in the context of a discussion related to a document exhibited in that case. And I note that when you were pressed on the issue you said: "I claim," at T5932, "with full responsibility and I am prepared to face the consequences if it proves to be true that Bascarsija was not targeted." And let me just check the cite for a second, Your Honours. I need to make sure that I've referred to this properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you upload that part so we can see that part as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The 65 ter number for that transcript is 1D26977, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, yes, just to remind you about the context. On the subject of shelling Bascarsija you were played a transcript of an intercepted conversation dated 28 May 1992 between General Ratko Mladic and one Mirko Vukasinovic and asked the question --

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Vukasinovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- and asked the question by my former colleague Mr. Waespi: "Mr. Veljovic, General Ratko Mladic, he was interested in the barracks, he was interested in firing at Bascarsija; right?" And your answer was: "You can hear that they should fire at Bascarsija but that did not happen. I claim with full responsibility and I'm prepared to face the consequences if it proves to be true that Bascarsija was targeted." Is it your assertion then that Bascarsija was never targeted by Sarajevo-Romanija Corps forces?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I claim this with full responsibility. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps never did that. There are even orders issued by General Milosevic that Bascarsija should not be targeted. Bascarsija is the biggest culture and historical monument that the city of Sarajevo has. It was built in Turkish times, and if only one 120-millimetre projectile had fallen on that, everything would have burnt because there are no hard materials there. That's why I claim with full responsibility and I invite experts to go there, and if they find that it is not the same as it was in the 1980s, then you can punish me. You can do an expert report on the paints, on the wood, everything the same. Sometimes people become euphoric and they issue certain orders, but there is the staff that alters those orders. So I can claim - and I do with full responsibility - that not a single projectile was ever fired on Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, you've given evidence here today that you know something about mortars, so you must know that mortars are anti-personnel weapons; correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, if I'm an officer there are certain things that I must know.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So let's have a look at P823. It's a report dated 3 November 1993. And there should be a translation into B/C/S available. So, Mr. Veljovic, this is a weekly BH political assessment drafted by UNPROFOR and an UNPROFOR civil affairs official on events in the region for the week of November 1993. And if we could go over to page 7 in the English and page 8 in the B/C/S, the first full paragraph on page 8. And the second paragraph on -- it's the second paragraph on the B/C/S page. Mr. Veljovic, contrary to what you've just told us, this document reports that Sarajevo and Gorazde have been under heavy bombardment in the past week. And in response to BH mortar fire, the old town of Sarajevo received almost 500 shells in a one-hour period on 27 October. And the old town, which has the highest percentage of Muslims in any Sarajevo area, is densely populated. Now, this contradicts what you've just told us with respect to shelling of Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't an operations officer in the SRK in 1993; I was in the brigade. But as for 500 shells, if they had fallen on the town they would have razed it to the ground. The entire Army of Republika Srpska didn't have 500 shells. I think this is grossly untrue. Five hundred shells to hit the old part of town, well, do you know what that means? What sort of inferno would have resulted from that? How many civilian casualties would there have been? The town of Sarajevo was never shelled in this way. Karadzic and Mladic prohibited this. But when you saw certain buildings on fire it was in 1992 when barracks were being protected which were in areas that were densely populated by Muslims. But to use 500 shells, well, what did we fire them from since at that time we didn't have that many launchers? It's quite impossible to understand how a human mind could have imagined such a thing. Five hundred shells, well, there would have been thousands of dead civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, Ms. Edgerton, could we clarify whether the old town of Sarajevo and Bascarsija refer to the same place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bascarsija is a smaller area. The old town includes Bistrik and Sedrenik. It's huge. It covers a very extensive surface, whereas Bascarsija is only one neighbourhood. This is really very interesting. Five hundred aerial bombs, well the Russians didn't drop that many bombs on Berlin.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, actually Mr. Veljovic is rather correct. Bascarsija is a local community next to Zajednica within Stari Grad, the old town. So it's one of several in that area and includes indeed some of the areas he's just mentioned, Bistrik, Sedrenik, and if I give further I might be doing it on the basis of my recollection and that wouldn't be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's move on. Yes, continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very sorry affair, this report here.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You talked a little bit in your statement about targeting. And you said legal military targets were the ones obtained through reconnaissance and intelligence from captured refugees or exchanged persons. So how -- what do you think is a legal military target?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: A legal military target, well, the demarcation lines or the forward defence line, any firing position regardless of whether it is located in or outside town. Since the Muslims were defending themselves at the edges of the town of Sarajevo, and according to the military establishment they had the artillery and the depth, we weren't allowed to fire on such targets. Although we knew about targets in Hrasno and Bascarsija and by the hospital, we didn't fire on these targets to avoid civilian casualties and especially in order to avoid killing children. So we couldn't fire into the depth because we wanted to avoid civilian casualties, although the other side took advantage of this. You can't put the artillery at the front line. It has to be positioned in the depth, and since the town was being defended they positioned their artillery in the depth and we couldn't fire on them. The only thing that could happen is if Sarajevo is semi-encircled and then we are assisted by units, if the gunpowder is wet when we're firing or if the information, the data, isn't correct, when you fire a shell then the shell doesn't reach the necessary range and hit the town. But it was forbidden to fire buildings in the town. The Supreme Command had forbidden this, and this command, this order went down to the lowest-level units. The command that the town shouldn't be targeted and that the artillery in urban neighbourhoods shouldn't be targeted either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I don't have anything further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Edgerton. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a few questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Veljovic, could you explain for the benefit of the Chamber whether the Podgrabski Battalion, the Jahorina and Trebevic Battalion, were located which -- this concerns the number of mortars, in fact, that your unit had?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The Podgrabski Battalion was facing Gorazde and the Jahorina one was facing Trnovo. And later, after Lukavica 93, that Jahorina Battalion was sent to the Nisic plateau to become part of the 1st Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. The Trebevic Battalion was on Trebevic and facing the town. It was in a forested area and it couldn't have opened infantry fire on the town from that area. It could have only opened fire on Muslim trenches which were also located in forested areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 48 you were asked who authorised the use of aerial bombs and it was suggested that the Main Staff as well as the corps commander authorised this. You said you didn't know about this but that it was possible. Do you have any information according to which the president of the republic authorised the use of aerial bombs or any other kinds of weapons?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I never heard any orders of any kind from the president, from the state, or from the Supreme Command. I only received orders from the corps command; they were conveyed through the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many municipalities are there in the old town in Sarajevo and are there any uninhabited areas?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: The municipality of the old town is very big and there are also rural areas within it as well as urban areas, so it is a very large municipality. It covers Trebevic which is also part of the old town, then Borci, Sedrenik, Vrace, Vucja Luka, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Although it's called the old town or Stari Grad it's not an urban area?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: It is partly urban, yes, and partly rural.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to ask you the following: Which -- what sort of fuel did these modified aerial bombs use?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: These aerial bombs used some sort of motors with rocket fuel and they travelled on rails or they were on rails that were on our lorries. The lorry would then raise its platform or lower the platform and this is how the device was used. It wasn't very precise. The Muslims called it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to ask you whether these rocket motors had tables of their own?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: They had --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- some kind of tables --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that goes beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The subject matter is precision. It doesn't go beyond the scope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the witness testified to the inaccuracy of the aerial bomb. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While you were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, did you hear or gain any insight into documents that the Main Staff sent to the president? Did you hear about such documents?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when I was in the corps since when the Main Staff sends reports to the Supreme Command, this would be sent down to the corps but not to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see this report that was shown to you according to which an aerial bomb was dropped on Hrasnica?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps not at that time. I wasn't in the corps command all the time. Sometimes I was on leave. Sometimes I had certain duties that I had to perform somewhere. So it wasn't possible for me to read through each and every report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you involved in the work that was carried out on building the modified aerial bombs?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not competent for such things. I'm an infantry officer. I don't know anything about rocket motors, metals, and so on and so forth. I did not participate in that. I'm not an expert on such matters. I'm not a technical expert by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you're not a ballistics expert either, are you? Do you have any ballistics training?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about whether these rockets were tested in the field or on training-grounds in Yugoslavia? Did you have any such information?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: There was never any such testing in the Yugoslav People's Army. This was the latest thing in the civil war. This wasn't part of the weapons of the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there training-ground in Yugoslavia where new weapons are tested?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is probably the case. There probably is some such training-ground. I think it must be near the Pasuljanske fields, in those areas, that's what I know from the media.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the following document, 1D8436 in the e-court system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know about the forces, the military forces, in Hrasnica, anything about their presence and infrastructure there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No. I know that there was a brigade in Hrasnica, or rather, that in the town of Sarajevo there was the 12th Division under the command of Fikret Pljevljak and the town of Sarajevo had the most numerous forces. That's where it was possible to mobilise the most men, the largest number of men, and experts who knew about certain technical issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I ask you to have a look at this analysis of the defence line. Could you tell the Chamber what period we are talking about and what it has to do, and pay particular attention to item 3, or rather, item 4, and (b) under 4. Could we zoom in or enlarge this for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Um, Your Honours, um, again I'm not yet sure how this arises from the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You showed the document which refers to the bombing of the centre of Hrasnica. That's the extent that I understand this line of questions. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour -- Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, please have a look at this proposal, have a look at item 4. What is this lieutenant-colonel suggesting with regard to retaliations because of groups, sabotage groups that are being infiltrated? Which military targets are being referred to?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it says the post office in Hrasnica, is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What does KM stand for?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: KM stands for command post. It's the command post of a given unit. I don't know whether it relates to a brigade, a battalion, a corps, or a division. KM is a military target, command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the KM of the 4th MTBR, MTBR does that stand for motorised brigade?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it's in the post office in Hrasnica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the post office KM. The KM of the 1st Mountain Brigade I suppose, the mountain home Hrasnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't ask you about these barracks. Under (b) it says business targets or economic targets? What does it say? Can you read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Economic facilities, the primary school in Hrasnica, production of shells, the production of shells in Hrasnica, Aleksa Santic primary school in Hrasnica, shell production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So is this also a legitimate military target?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, but it was difficult for us to decide to fire on such targets because we were afraid of killing civilians. We only fired on the demarcation lines, but there was a margin of error, 50 metres. It all depended on psychological factors, on the target person, on the charge, on the calibre of the barrel not being appropriate for the shell. Then you have to use plastic shells. The gases aren't appropriate for expelling the projectile. Many errors can be made in the artillery. In France in the first world war, 10.000 soldiers were killed by their own artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell the Chamber when it was determined that there were such targets in the centre of Hrasnica, could you tell us anything about the dates?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Well, 0508 of -- the 5th of August, 1994, at the time I wasn't in the corps so I couldn't say anything. At the time I was in the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade. I was at the Nisic plateau. I was in command of two battalions, the Sokolac and the Jahorina battalion. That was during this period of time. I wasn't in the corps command. I was in the corps command as of the 19th of December, 1994, but here I see that it's the 5th of August, 1994. So I couldn't say anything because that wasn't close to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that as of that date up to 1995 the centre of Hrasnica was ever targeted, although they were aware of the installations and the legitimate targets there?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that that was ever targeted. We always knew that they were making those things, that they placed their command posts in the schools, and we knew that if we targeted them that we would inflict civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the witness please be asked to come closer to the microphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That that will be admitted as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D2353.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Veljovic, when answering the questions could you speak to the microphone? For example, I take it that you can come a bit closer to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us to what extent were you familiar with aerial bombs; i.e., those modified aerial bombs? How familiar were you with them? What was your participation in all of that?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: I was not well informed about those aerial bombs. Several of our brigades had those aerial bombs: The 1st Romanija didn't have them; the 1st Sarajevo didn't have them; the 2nd Sarajevo didn't have them; the Ilidza had them; the Iljas Brigade had them; the Vogosca and the others that had facilities nearby such as the Pretis institute, the maintenance depot, they made them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your brigade have them?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: No. My brigade, which was the 4th Sarajevo Light Infantry Brigade, didn't have them, nor did the 1st Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you participate in the launch of that bomb?

utterances.speaker: STEVAN VELJOVIC
utterances.text: Only in the Trnovo theatre of war around Treskavica I saw the bomb being launched, but it is wilderness. There are no settlements there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Veljovic, for your testimony. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Veljovic. On behalf of the Chamber I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will take a break so we'll rise all together. We'll break for 45 minutes and will resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.26 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up 1D6041 in e-court. This is Mr. Maksimovic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Have you read this statement? Have you reviewed it, Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you sign it as well?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it accurately reflect what you stated?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were -- we have to wait for the interpretation. If I were to put the same questions to you today and offer your answers in lieu of the statement, would your answers be the same as they are in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I would like to tender this 92 ter package into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any objection, Ms. Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: His Rule 92 ter statement as well as five associated exhibits will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the statement 65 ter number 1D06041 will be Exhibit D2354.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The other associated exhibits' number will be given in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to read a short summary of Mr. Maksimovic's statement. I'm going to do it in English. [In English] In May 1992 Sinisa Maksimovic became a member of the communications platoon of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on Tvrdimici, until September 1992 when he was transferred to the Igman's Brigade's 4th Infantry Battalion in Blazuj. In January 1993 he became a member of intervention platoon of the Igman Brigade. In the summer of 1993 he took part in the operation to occupy the hills of Golo Brdo, Obeljak, and Stupnik, all dominant positions from which the Muslim forces fired at and shelled Hadzici. His conclusion is that in these units there were people who had been convicts. During this operation his brigade took the position on Brezovaca on Igman. The Tresnjevo Brdo hill was also taken but his unit withdrew under superior command's order. They were promised that these positions would be occupied by UNPROFOR and not Muslim forces. Immediately after withdrawal the Tresnjevo Brdo hill was occupied by Muslim forces, situation that remained unchanged until the end of the war. In June 1994, after having completed his schooling in the first class -- at the first class college for officers and being given the rank of 2nd lieutenant, Sinisa Maksimovic was transferred to the 1st Romanija Brigade of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. He was accompanied company commander in Mrkovici in July 1994. All fire was aimed at the enemy lines of -- all fire -- devices of this brigade -- company were on the enemy lines which were very close to theirs, at a distance from 20 to 100 metres. Almost all soldiers in this company were local men, among whom the dominant conviction was that the Markale I incident had been engineered by the enemy. The units opposed to his were from the 105 Brigade -- Mountain Brigade of 1st Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Muslim forces possessed sniper weapons. Muslim special units "Laste" took Spicasta Stijena at least once, in mid-September 1994. In late 1994 he was transferred to the Igman Brigade. In August 1995 a systematic bombing of and artillery assault on Serb positions was initiated by the UN Rapid Reaction Force stationed in the Igman-Bjelasnica sector. Sinisa Maksimovic watched the UN Rapid Reaction Forces, positioned in Muslim-controlled territory, transport heavy weaponry along the road over Igman. This assault had air support from a large number of aircrafts. The Muslim forces also opened fire but dared not launch an infantry assault due to the intensity of the UN artillery and aircraft fire. Regarding incident in Sedrenik area on 17th of April of 1993, the positions of Sinisa Maksimovic's unit remained unchanged even before his arrival as a company commander. Associated document 1D08572 shows the area where his unit was located in the woods. Regarding incident Sedrenik area on 6th of March, 1995, and to the best of Sinisa Maksimovic's knowledge, Serb units at that location did not have trained snipers in their ranks. The units were comprised of local people who were not trained for sniper fire. The alleged positions from which the sniper attack in Sedrenik was allegedly carried out were under constant enemy fire. Regarding incident occurred in the junction of Sedrenik Street and Redzepa Gorusanovica Street on 22nd November 1994, and beside the argument put forward in connection to the aforementioned incidents, Sinisa Maksimovic ask that he never issued any order for civilians to be fired upon, nor did he ever received any information that civilian targets had been fired upon by members of his unit. That would be a short summary and I do not have questions for that witness at this point of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have a couple of questions about your evidence, the evidence set out in your statement, and they're actually in regard to the incidents you spoke about in paragraphs 7, 8, and 9 of your statement. So in paragraph 7 you were asked some questions about an address at Sedrenik 157. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the question that was put to me. However, I'm not familiar with the address, Sedrenik 157 --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be provided with his statement in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to have your statement in front of you, Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have a copy, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I'm just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Or we can print it up thanks to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Great. Now, if you could just flip over to paragraph 7, there you were asked some questions with respect to an incident at an address at Sedrenik 157. And when you were asked those questions, were you told that this incident took place on 17 April 1993?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was told that the incident had happened in the month of April and that I was not the company commander in Mrkovici at that time. I was also told that I should look at the pictures, the photos, the map, and to point at the positions of my units. To my knowledge, those positions had not changed and did not change after I became the company commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 8 you were asked some questions about an incident dated 6 March 1995. You weren't company commander in Mrkovici at that period of time either, were you?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I was not company commander at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I assist. The witness said that the lines were not changed either before or thereafter, which is why he was asked to talk about that. That's on lines 9 and 10. The witness said that the lines had not changed before he joined or after he joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said that and then you can take up that issue in your re-examination. Please refrain as far as possible, Mr. Karadzic. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the third incident you were asked questions about in paragraph 9, were you told that Dr. Karadzic is not charged with that incident?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't told that. I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now in your statement and I think -- and in relation to the situation at Sedrenik generally, you talked about the ABiH holding a position between -- beneath Spicaste Stijene and you've talked about whether or not your unit opens sniper fire from Spicaste Stijene. Is it your evidence today that SRK units at that area did not shoot from Spicaste Stijene at all?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say that. We did open fire when necessary when we were attacked. Of course we fired. However, our activities were aimed at the enemy positions, exclusively at the enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe you could answer a question I have then about a document that we've received in evidence here, P1619, please. It's a report prepared by UNMO Sector Sarajevo on 6 March 1995 and it's been translated into B/C/S. I'll just wait until we can see the version in your language. Wonderful. Thank you. If we could jump over to English page 3 in both versions -- sorry, English and B/C/S page 3, paragraph 8, sub a, sub ii and iii. There we see reports on the wounding of two civilians on 6 March from Sharpstone. One is a male aged 48 and the other is a male aged 14. Now if we could jump back over to page 1, paragraph 3(b), I'd like you to have a look at that. Now, paragraph 3(b) says after these incidents that I've just referred to the UN EgyptBat anti-sniping APC at that location returned fire onto Bosnian Serb army positions at Sharpstone. And following this retaliation, the UNMO Vogosca team received a telephone call from the commander Radava Battalion, Vogosca Brigade, Bosnian Serb army, stating that if the EgyptBat APC in his target practice area (Sedrenik) is not removed within 30 minutes it will be fired upon. And shortly after this call the sector commander arrived at the APC location. The UNMO Vogosca team received another telephone call shortly thereafter from the Radava Battalion commander stating that he would also fire on the UNPROFOR reinforcements with the APC and the APC was then moved to a safer position. And I wonder if that affects your answer in any regard.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't affect it. Those things happened in 1995 when I was not in the command of the Mirkovic company. I can't say that the report is not correct, I can't say that. However, as for what was happening then I can't talk about that because I was not present in the unit at that time. That was March 1995 and already in December 1994 I was transferred to the Igman Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll move on to the incident you discussed at paragraph 7 in your statement. You were shown a photograph and it has the 65 ter number 1D8572, and you were told that that photograph was taken from the approximate place where the alleged victim of the incident was located, and you made some markings on that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I wonder if we could call that photograph up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Once you've had a look at that, I'd like to show you another photograph that was taken from the actual incident location, and it's 65 ter number 9563A [sic].

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And maybe we could display those two photographs side by side on the computer monitor. And, by the way 9536A is a still image taken from the 360-degree image that was admitted through Barry Hogan as P2207. Page 2 now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this photo 9536A, page 2, is a photo of the Sharpstone area taken from the actual incident location. And I wonder if having those two photos side by side that changes your answer and the markings you made in any regard.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I would like an explanation of this photo, F2. I can see two houses there. I can see some trees. And in the background I can see one part of a hill but not too well. I don't know what you want me to say based on the right-hand side photo. I marked the left-hand side photo. I put a rectangular sign to show where my units were not, whereas the circular sign marks Spicaste Stijene. I don't recognise any of those things in the other photo, in F2.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, this Chamber has received evidence that this photograph was taken from the actual incident location and the small green triangle, upside down triangle that you see, the hilltop in the distance, is the alleged origin of fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And if we can zoom in to that triangle. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: On 65 ter number 9536A, you see that it displays a different area than the one that you've marked and the photo was taken from a different angle than the picture that you've marked in 1D8572.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Again, can I have an explanation with regard to the left-hand side house. Is that the same house that we can see in the other photo where I marked the position of my unit?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes, okay. In that case I can't say anything about the position from which it was allegedly fired because it doesn't seem to belong to the area of responsibility of my company. It seems to me that that position is a bit further to the right from the end of the zone of responsibility of my company, and if this is the assumed direction from which the bullets arrived, then I can say that this did not belong to the Mokrovici Company. That bullet must have belonged to another unit that was our neighbour on the left flank.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And since this photograph is already part of an exhibit we're not going to tender it and just move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 8 of your statement you said -- answering questions about the incident that took place on 6 March 1995 that Serb positions from the alleged incident locations were more than a thousand metres away. I'd like to ask you about that. Did you get told the address of the incident location?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know the address. The address would not have meant much to me anyway when it came to the positioning of the location or the way I understood it, the location of the incident, that is. What I could see in the photo was something that I assumed must have been very far from our positions. I don't know if you understand my answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think I do. Your estimate of a thousand metres is an assumption based on a photo you were shown; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now for the last question, and also in relation to this incident, you said your units - I imagine referring to the time you were in the Mrkovici company - your units had 7.62-millimetre automatic rifles whose efficacy was no less than 800 metres in relation to the target; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. However, it was a bit exaggerated. Eight hundred metre is a lot for the efficacy of the rifle. It is most efficient at 3- to 400 metres. Eight hundred metres would be the ultimate distance for which it can be assumed that that rifle could hit its target. Eight hundred metres is much too much. I made a mistake there. Being familiar with the automatic rifles and automatic weaponry, I would say that its true efficiency range is at some 300 to 400 metres. That's its quality efficiency range.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you also had 7.9-millimetre weapons and ammunition; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think that there was an M53 machine-gun in the unit. I can't remember which location exactly. The entire company had about 12 to 13 trenches or fortified positions. As to where the machine-gun was located exactly, I could not say. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Maybe -- let's maybe have a look at one last document while we're talking about fire-arms like this. 65 ter number 23826. And while we're waiting for that to come up, what's the effective range of an M53 machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that it would be between 7- and 800 metres. An M53 machine-gun is extremely unreliable. It's an unreliable weapon. Bullets often get jammed. When you open fire from such a machine-gun the result is very imprecise, in fact. The machine-gun is used to fire bursts of fire. I think the enemy is more affected by the bursts of fire than by the results achieved by the machine-gun fire itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one last document dated 29 October 1993, and it's a document from the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade to the Sarajevo Corps command responding to a query from the corps commander and indicating that in the brigade they had M76, 7.9-millimetre sniper rifles; M48, 7.9-millimetre sniper rifles; M59/66, 7.62-millimetre sniper rifles. Are you familiar with the effective ranges of these three types of sniper rifles that I've just described?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think the 7.9, the M76, has a range of 1.000 metres, an effective range of 1.000 metres. As for the other two sniper rifles, the M48 and 59, the M59/66, I'm not sure about the range of these two weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could we have this as a Prosecution exhibit, please, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P5945, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just one last question and it's relating to the last sentence in paragraph 10 of your statement. You referred to the Laste, the Bosnian special unit, taking Spicaste Stijene in mid-September 1994. That only lasted for a couple of days, didn't it? Your forces recovered the ridge a couple of days after that; correct?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a few questions, Your Excellency. Could we have a look at P5945 just to see if the title -- to see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Maksimovic, could you please just read out the first part --

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Intensifying sniping activity against Muslim forces to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, the command of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you graduated from the college for officers, could you tell us whether the Muslim forces are legitimate target for snipers?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: The ABiH was a legitimate target. The Muslim forces were a legitimate target. The title is a bit strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what we have here, was it possible to target civilians? Could snipers target the civilians?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Could I read through all of this? I don't know what is at stake. Is this a report? I'm not sure what the nature of this document is. It's not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Read out the first sentence. I think that's quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a report. Could you please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does this document allow for snipers to target civilians? Does it imply that such action could be taken?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Of course not because a report is a document that is sent to the superior command and it reports on the situation in the unit, on situation with regard to materiel and technical equipment, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at Prosecution Exhibit P2193. Could we zoom into the top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this map, the map of the town?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's Sarajevo and its surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Defence team showed you a different map that the Prosecution marked this map, it marked the locations of incidents 2, 13, and 17. Can you locate Sedrenik, Groblje, Skajca [phoen], Sokak. Do you recognise these places and can you tell us how far are the locations where these incidents occurred were located from your positions?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: Quite far. Incident number 2 I think is about -- or the location of that incident is at a distance of 800 metres to a kilometre roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to underscore, as I said earlier, this -- with the witness, incident 2 -- pardon me, incident 13 was dropped from the indictment against Karadzic. He's no longer charged with that. And I let the paragraph referring to that incident in the witness's statement go in because I thought in context it was the fair thing to do. But I just wanted to remind Dr. Karadzic, before we go down that road, that he can't have a kick at the can, so to speak, with a dropped incident, particularly since the Prosecution was precluded from referring to dropped incidents in our case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But you have no difficult with F2 -- 2nd and 17th incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, can you see the main street in the Sedrenik neighbourhood here and can you tell us whether it was possible for you to target these locations, location number 2 and location number 17?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is very difficult to provide you with any specific answers on the basis of this map. Sedrenik is a densely populated area and as for the location of the street where incident number 2 occurred, I believe that could be the main street that led to Mrkovici. As for incidents 17 and 13, or rather, incident number 17, if I can see this clearly I think that it is located beneath Trdonje -- Grdonj. And it would be difficult to say that it was a visible location from my positions. The top of the Grdonj hill was not under our control, the top of the Grdonj hill. So incident number 17, as far as that incident is concerned I wouldn't say that it occurred because it was targeted from our positions because it is beneath Grdonj. As for incident number 2, the location is quite a distance from the line itself. So if such a incident occurred it would be difficult to say that it was a deliberate hit fired from our positions. It's difficult to say whether fire was opened from our positions in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the altitude of the hill of Grdonj in relation to the positions of your company and Sedrenik?

utterances.speaker: SINISA MAKSIMOVIC
utterances.text: It's a dominant position, it's above Sedrenik, and part of the Grdonj hill at the level of Mala Kula, if you have a look at the map it's to the north of the hill, at the level of Mala Kula that is, in fact, where my units were located, or rather, my company and platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Maksimovic. On behalf of this Chamber I'd like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there anything to raise? Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I would just like to put on the record the fact that the next witness that we had scheduled to testify who had been designated as KW-341 declined to testify after being notified that the Chamber had denied our motion for protective measures. And so he will not be called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So who is the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness I am referring to is K --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, who will be testifying?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness to be testifying on Tuesday, the 30th of October, is Colonel Steven Joudry and we filed a witness list today for that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Robinson. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to belabour this point, but I'm not entirely sure why it was necessary to put that on the record, but if it is to be intended to be a suggestion that the Trial Chamber's failure to provide protective measures were somehow -- were a reflection of the nature of the witness's concerns in not testifying, I feel obliged to say the Prosecution doesn't accept that insinuation. We consider that the witness would have been subjected to cross-examination of a nature that he didn't want exposed to the public and that's the nature of the failure to appear now. And if we continue this discussion, I'd be more than happy to discuss that evidence in more detail. Secondly, I also wanted to address a comment that was made the other day to the effect that no Prosecution witnesses ever had protective measures sought ultimately denied; that is simply not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us leave it at that. Unless there are any other things to be raised, the hearing is now adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 30th day of October, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.08 p.m.,
